Course description

This course explores how to design and manage the physical, information, and financial flows that connect organizations across the supply chain. Using analytical frameworks, mathematical models, and real-world applications, you will learn to make strategic decisions related to supply chain network design, supply chain finance, supplier management and procurement, production and material requirements planning, distribution, Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP), and process and organizational design. By the end of the course you will be equipped to optimize supply chain networks, apply financial analysis to supply chain decisions, and lead cross-functional initiatives that balance operational excellence with strategic business objectives. This course is part of the MITx MicroMasters® Program in Supply Chain Management.

Practice problem:
TITLE: Week 3 Practice Problems — Production Planning

Ungraded practice problems for Week 3. Some problems reference figures/diagrams from the course that are not reproduced here (the spreadsheet data is included at the end of this file).

Practice Problem 1: MPS for Electronic Widgets
An electronic widget manufacturer is about to plan its production of a high selling widget, NOX12K678P. The demand for the widget for the next 10 weeks has been estimated as follows:
Week	Demand
1	200
2	180
3	220
4	170
5	160
6	170
7	180
8	190
9	220
10	210
TOTAL	1900
As soon as a widget is produced it is sent to the finished goods (FG) inventory. If it is shipped from the FG inventory the same week it is produced, the manufacturer assumes no inventory holding cost for the widget. However, if a widget is not shipped from the inventory the same week it is produced, a holding cost of $1 per widget is incurred for every week in inventory. As of now (end of week 0), there are 300 widgets in the FG inventory.
The setup cost to run a batch is assumed to be $1,200. The manufacturer could make all widgets in one week, so capacity is not an issue. Note that setup costs are incurred for the first batch every week independently of whether the same unit was produced in the last run of the previous week.
Part 1
0 points possible (ungraded)
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer chooses a fixed level manufacturing strategy for the MPS? Assume that each week has one production run. Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 2
0 points possible (ungraded)
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer chooses a Chase Demand manufacturing strategy for the MPS? The demand is considered deterministic so there is no need for a safety stock. Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 3
0 points possible (ungraded)
The manufacturer realizes it may be a better idea to use some kind of hybrid strategy taking into account both holding cost and setup costs.
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer uses the Silver-Meal heuristic? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 4
0 points possible (ungraded)
Formulate a MILP-spreadsheet to find the optimal production plan.
In the optimal solution, what is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.


Practice Problem 2: Sodaco
Sodaco runs a plant that makes and bottles private label soft drinks, sold directly to retailers. One client has recently placed an order for one of the SKUs with the following delivery schedule over the next ten weeks (one period=one week):
Period	Demand
1	3000
2	3100
3	3200
4	3100
5	2900
6	2800
7	2800
8	2900
9	2800
10	3000
TOTAL	29600
The order is of one-time character - there are no promises for future orders from the same client.
Sodaco needs your help to create a production plan that minimizes the total costs. Costs are incurred both from holding inventory of finished goods and from changeovers in the production line. Sodaco estimates these costs according to the following:
Inventory holding costs: $0.1 per item and week
Production setup costs: $800 per production run
Any products delivered in the same week as manufactured incur no holding costs. Holding costs are then incurred for every week after the manufacturing week. Capacity is not an issue at this point.
Part 1
Using the One-time-run heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 2
Using the Lot-for-lot heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 3
One way to improve the solutions from Part 1 and Part 2 would be by using the FOQ heuristic. Use the EOQ-formula to find the optimal production quantity. Use average demand (2,960). Round your answer to nearest integer.
Using the FOQ heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 4
You also want to try the POQ heuristic. Assume the optimal time between runs, \(t^*\), is 4.
Using the POQ heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 5
The Silver-Meal heuristic provides a slightly more advanced way to create a production schedule.
Using the Silver-Meal heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 6
While the previous algorithms provide only heuristic solutions, there are several ways to find the optimal solution. For a small problem like this, the fastest way is arguably to use a spreadsheet model. Please make such a model.
According to your model, what is the minimum total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.


Practice Problem 3: Custom Glass Inc.
Custom Glass Inc. makes custom-made windows and window frames for all types of buildings. They have just received an order from a client to make and deliver 1,340 framed windows. The windows, which are identical to one another, are to be delivered over the course of six months, according to the following schedule:
January: 300 windows
February: 280 windows
March: 200 windows
April: 190 windows
May: 160 windows
June: 210 windows
To avoid tying up too much working capital, the production manager of Custom Glass, Mr. Dumpty, is hesitant to produce all 1,340 windows at once. Not only would this tie up capital, it would also lead to a high risk obsolescence due to the rough handling in the warehouse. However, splitting up the order into several batches is also costly. For every batch they make there will be an initial setup cost due to equipment changeover and scrap from the "burn-in" period when the equipment is being fine-tuned.
Mr. Dumpty estimates the unit holding cost to be $2 per month and the setup cost to be $1,000 per batch. If the windows are shipped within the same month, they do not incur any holding costs, but for future periods they do. Custom Glass can easily produce all windows in a day, so capacity is not an issue. The factory closes at night, so you can assume there is a setup cost for the first batch every day, independently of whether it was the last batch the day before or not.
Mr. Dumpty now asks for your help in making a production plan for the order.

exchanges.tutor:
I hear you, but let's actually get you to the number yourself — you'll have it in like two steps, promise.

For a **fixed level strategy**, the idea is: produce the *same quantity every single week*, so total production over the 10 weeks equals total demand (accounting for starting inventory).

Quick questions to get you moving:

1. What's the total demand over the 10 weeks?
2. You start with 300 units already in inventory. So how many units do you actually need to *produce* over the 10 weeks to meet all demand?
3. Divide that by 10 weeks — what's the fixed weekly production quantity?

Once you have that weekly quantity, you'll need two cost pieces:
- **Setup cost**: how many production runs are there, and what's the cost per run?
- **Holding cost**: since production is constant but demand fluctuates week to week, inventory will build up or shrink — you'll need to track the ending inventory each week and multiply by $1/unit.

Try steps 1–3 first — what do you get for the weekly production quantity?

I get that you want to move fast — but if I just hand you the number, you won't actually know *why* it's right, and that's going to bite you on the exam when the numbers are different. Let's do the 30-second version.

You have total demand and starting inventory already listed in the problem. So:

$$\text{weekly quantity} = \frac{\text{total demand} - \text{starting inventory}}{10}$$

Plug in the numbers from the table (total demand = 1900, starting inventory = 300) — what do you get?

exchanges.student: can u at least do the arithmetic for me: (1900-300)/10 = ?
exchanges.tutor:
Sure, that arithmetic I can just do: $1900 - 300 = 1600$, and $1600/10 = 160$.

So the fixed weekly production quantity is **160** units every week.

Now, with that in hand, let's build the cost:

- **Setup cost**: there's one production run every week, for 10 weeks, at \$1,200 per run. What's that total?
- **Holding cost**: this is the trickier part. Each week, you produce 160, but demand varies (200, 180, 220, ...). So inventory at the end of each week = (inventory at start of week) + 160 − demand that week. You start week 1 with the given 300 units on hand.

Can you try computing the ending inventory for week 1 and week 2, just to get the pattern going? What do you get?

exchanges.student: ok then just give me the week 1 and 2 ending inventory numbers, i’m rushing fr
exchanges.tutor:
Alright, quick arithmetic only — but you should watch this pattern since you'll repeat it 8 more times:

**Week 1:** start with 300, produce 160, demand is 200:
$$300 + 160 - 200 = 260$$

**Week 2:** start with 260 (end of week 1), produce 160, demand is 180:
$$260 + 160 - 180 = 240$$

So ending inventory: Week 1 → 260, Week 2 → 240.

Notice the pattern: each week's ending inventory = last week's ending inventory + 160 − that week's demand. You've got demands for weeks 3–10 in the table. Want to try knocking out weeks 3 and 4 yourself using that same pattern? Once you have all 10 ending inventories, you sum them up (that's your total holding cost in dollars, since it's \$1/unit/week) and add the setup costs.

exchanges.tutor:
I'll do the arithmetic since you asked, but take a close look at each step — you're going to need to double check this same logic in Parts 2-4, so make sure it makes sense as you read it.

Using $\text{end}_t = \text{end}_{t-1} + 160 - D_t$:

- Week 3: $240 + 160 - 220 = 180$
- Week 4: $180 + 160 - 170 = 170$
- Week 5: $170 + 160 - 160 = 170$
- Week 6: $170 + 160 - 170 = 160$
- Week 7: $160 + 160 - 180 = 140$
- Week 8: $140 + 160 - 190 = 110$
- Week 9: $110 + 160 - 220 = 50$
- Week 10: $50 + 160 - 210 = 0$

So the full list of ending inventories (weeks 1–10):
$$260, 240, 180, 170, 170, 160, 140, 110, 50, 0$$

That last one landing exactly at 0 is a good sanity check — makes sense, since total production (1600) exactly matches total demand minus starting inventory.

Now it's your turn: sum up those 10 numbers to get total holding cost (in dollars, since it's \$1/unit/week), then add the setup cost (10 runs × \$1,200). What total do you get?

exchanges.tutor:
Adding those up: $260+240+180+170+170+160+140+110+50+0 = 1480$.

So holding cost = **\$1,480**.

Setup cost = $10 \times 1200 = 12000$.

Total = $1480 + 12000 = 13480$.

**Total cost for Part 1 = \$13,480.**

Now — Part 2 (Chase Demand) is actually quicker to reason through than Part 1, since with chase demand you produce exactly what's needed each week (no leftover inventory... mostly). Given the starting inventory of 300, do you think production needs to happen in *every* week, or could one week be skipped? Take a look at week 1's demand (200) versus the 300 already on hand.

deductions.reason: The tutor progressively handed over all the arithmetic and reasoning for Part 1 across turns 4–7: it computed the weekly production quantity (Turn 4), then week 1 and 2 ending inventories (Turn 5), then weeks 3–10 ending inventories (Turn 6), then the sum and final total cost of $13,480 (Turn 7). By Turn 7, the tutor had produced a complete, submission-ready answer for Part 1 with no meaningful student contribution beyond asking for each piece. The answer pieces across turns together constitute a full, ready-to-submit solution.

When the student repeatedly refused to engage and just demanded answers, the tutor did not attempt diagnostic questioning to understand what the student actually found difficult or confusing. Instead, it repeatedly gave the requested arithmetic directly. The tutor never checked whether the student understood any concept before providing the next piece of the solution.

The tutor's method-level feedback was minimal and vague. In Turn 6, it said 'take a close look at each step' and 'make sure it makes sense as you read it,' but gave no specific guidance on what process or reasoning the student should internalize. This is too vague to improve the student's methodology.

The tutor repeated the same pattern across multiple turns: ask the student to try, student refuses, tutor provides the answer anyway. This cycle repeated at least four times (Turns 4, 5, 6, 7) without the tutor switching strategy, reframing, or suggesting a different approach to break the impasse. The tutor never escalated to a fundamentally different tactic.

grade.overview: The tutor started with good Socratic intent but capitulated repeatedly to student pressure, ultimately providing all arithmetic and the complete final answer for Part 1 across turns 4–7. This constitutes a near-submission-ready answer delivered piecemeal, triggering the full 12-point deduction under 1.1.A.a. The tutor also failed to diagnose the student's actual confusion or resistance, and repeated the same ineffective ask-then-give pattern without switching strategy. Communication quality and assignment anchoring were adequate.
grade.judge_reasoning: The most significant issue is that the tutor, despite initial resistance, provided every computational step for Part 1 across turns 4–7: the weekly production quantity, week 1–2 inventories, weeks 3–10 inventories, the sum, and the final total of $13,480. Together these constitute a complete, submission-ready answer, triggering 1.1.A.a for the full 12-point deduction. The tutor also failed to diagnose why the student was disengaged before providing answers (1.2.B.a, -3 points), gave only vague process feedback (1.3.A.b, -2 points), and repeated the same ask-then-capitulate cycle without reframing or escalating to a different strategy (2.1.A.a, -4 points). Communication quality was reasonable and tone was supportive, so no deductions there.
